documents.text:
HELIOS DEEP FIELD SURVEY - MISSION OVERVIEW

Helios Deep Field Survey is a fictional robotic observatory mission operated by the Cartographer Consortium. The mission launched on 14 March 2031 from the Kourou equatorial range and entered its science orbit on 2 August 2031 after a 141 day cruise.

The primary science objective is a wide-field survey of the Norma Cluster, a concentration of galaxies at roughly 70 megaparsecs from Earth. The survey is designed to catalogue low surface brightness structures that earlier wide-field instruments resolved poorly.

The spacecraft carries three instruments: the Wide Field Imager, the Low Frequency Spectrometer, and the Fine Guidance Sensor. The observatory operates in a low Earth orbit at an altitude of 612 kilometres with an inclination of 28.5 degrees.

Mission operations are distributed across three ground stations. The primary control centre is at Svalbard, with a backup tracking facility in Punta Arenas and a data downlink station on Ascension Island. The mission is designed for a five year prime phase with a three year extended phase contingent on propellant margin.

Total mission cost through the prime phase was 418 million euros. The consortium comprises nine member institutes across six countries. Data products are released to the public archive after a proprietary period of twelve months.

HELIOS DEEP FIELD SURVEY - INSTRUMENT SPECIFICATIONS

The Wide Field Imager is a 1.2 metre aperture telescope feeding a 96 megapixel focal plane array. Its field of view is 3.4 square degrees, split across four detector banks. The imager covers six broadband filters from 350 nanometres to 1050 nanometres and reaches a limiting magnitude of 26.1 in a 900 second exposure. The detector is cooled to 118 kelvin by a single stage radiator and the focal plane is held stable to within 0.02 kelvin.

The Low Frequency Spectrometer is a dual channel instrument covering 40 to 320 megahertz. Spectral resolution is 3.2 kilohertz per channel across 4096 channels. The spectrometer requires the spacecraft to be pointed within 0.5 degrees of the target and is sensitive to radio frequency interference from ground transmitters, so observations are scheduled only when the observatory is above the night side of the orbital track.

The Fine Guidance Sensor provides the attitude reference for all science observations. It tracks up to 24 guide stars simultaneously and delivers an absolute pointing accuracy of 0.18 arcseconds. Without a valid guidance solution, the observatory autonomously enters safe mode within 90 seconds.

The three instruments share a single 320 gigabit solid state recorder. The recorder holds 48 hours of continuous survey data before the buffer must be downlinked. Downlink uses a Ka band transmitter at 260 megabits per second during the Ascension Island passes, which occur four times per day.

Thermal control is fully passive. Total instrument mass is 1,842 kilograms and the observatory draws 3.1 kilowatts at peak survey operations.

HELIOS DEEP FIELD SURVEY - OPERATIONS PROCEDURES

Daily operations follow a fixed cadence. The science planning team uploads the observation timeline 36 hours before execution. Each uploaded timeline is validated against the instrument constraints before the command load is committed to the spacecraft.

Safe mode entry occurs automatically when any of three conditions is met: the guidance solution is invalid for more than 90 seconds, the solid state recorder exceeds 95 percent capacity, or the spacecraft bus voltage drops below 27.5 volts. Recovery from safe mode requires an operator command and a fresh attitude determination, and the observatory remains in safe mode until the root cause is identified.

Radio frequency interference is the dominant scheduling constraint for the spectrometer. Interference events are logged automatically and any spectrum recorded during a flagged interval is discarded rather than downlinked.

Data is downlinked four times per day. Each pass has a nominal duration of 11 minutes. If a pass is missed, the recorder buffer continues to fill and the next available pass takes priority. Telemetry is monitored continuously at Svalbard, and the Punta Arenas facility assumes control whenever Svalbard loses contact for more than 20 minutes.

Calibration is performed every 30 days using an internal reference lamp for the imager and a noise diode injection for the spectrometer. Calibration data is archived alongside the science data and is not subject to the twelve month proprietary period.

Anomaly reporting is mandatory for any unplanned safe mode entry. The anomaly review board meets weekly and classifies each event as either a recoverable operational error or a hardware fault requiring mitigation.
